"'''Metalhead'''" is the fifth episode of the fourth season of the anthology series ''[[Black Mirror]]''. It was written by series creator [[Charlie Brooker]] and directed by [[David Slade]]. The episode first aired on [[Netflix]], along with the rest of series four, on 29 December 2017.

"Metalhead" is filmed in [[black and white]], and it follows the plight of Bella ([[Maxine Peake]]) trying to flee from robotic "dogs" after the unexplained [[societal collapse|collapse]] of human society. The dogs were influenced by [[Boston Dynamics]]' robots such as [[BigDog]]. Filming took place in England, with [[Lidar]] scans used for scenes from the dog's perspective. Lasting 41 minutes, "Metalhead" is the second-shortest episode behind "[[Mazey Day (Black Mirror)|Mazey Day]]".

Reviews were mostly positive. It has been compared to ''[[The Terminator]]'', as both works feature machines chasing humans. The episode's message has been widely debated, with reviewers discussing questions about [[artificial intelligence]] and the final shot of a box of teddy bears. The plot and short running time have received mixed reviews, while Peake's acting and Slade's directing have been praised, along with the cinematography and the design of the dogs.

==Plot==
In a desolate landscape, Bella ([[Maxine Peake]]), Anthony (Clint Dyer), and Clarke (Jake Davies) drive to a warehouse searching for something to help ease the pain of Jack, who is dying. While Clarke [[hot-wiring|hot-wires]] a van, Bella and Anthony break into the warehouse. They find the box they are looking for, but behind it is a four-legged robotic guard—a "dog". The dog sprays Bella and Anthony with shrapnel that contains trackers, then climbs down and shoots Anthony dead. Bella flees without the box to her car, with Clarke following in the van. The dog jumps into the van, kills Clarke and pursues Bella. It eventually enters her car, but the car teeters off a cliff when she escapes.

Bella uses pliers to extract the tracker embedded in her leg. Over her walkie-talkie, she asks someone to pass a message to her loved ones in case she is killed. Bella is chased by the dog into a forest, climbing a nearby tree. The dog's forelimb was damaged in the car wreck, so it cannot climb the tree, and instead powers down and waits. Bella drains it of power by repeatedly throwing sweets at it, causing it to power up and down. When the dog no longer responds, Bella climbs down. She finds a compound and breaks in.

Bella takes car keys and a shotgun from two rotting corpses in the bedroom. When the sun rises, the dog recharges and gains access to the compound. As the dog approaches, Bella leaps out and throws paint over its visual sensor, then throws the paint can to the corner of the room to distract it and hurries to the car. However, the car will not start, so she turns on the radio and hides. As the dog investigates the noise, Bella shoots it. The dog stabs her in the leg; she shoots it again and it falls to the ground. The dog releases an air-burst shell, showering Bella with tracker-embedded shrapnel.

In the bathroom mirror, Bella sees many trackers in her face. She lifts a knife, but notices a tracker in her [[jugular vein]]. Bella speaks into her walkie-talkie, unsure if she can be heard, saying goodbye to her loved ones. As she puts the knife to her throat, the camera pans out over the landscape, showing dogs approaching and investigating. In the warehouse, the box's contents—dozens of [[teddy bear]]s—have spilled onto the floor.

"Metalhead" is the second-shortest episode of ''Black Mirror'', with a length of 41 minutes<ref name="variety interview"/> (at 40 minutes, "[[Mazey Day (Black Mirror)|Mazey Day]]" is the shortest).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cosmopolitan.com/uk/entertainment/a44170793/netflix-black-mirror-mazey-day-episode-explained/|title=Netflix's Black Mirror: Mazey Day episode explained|work=[[Cosmopolitan (magazine)|Cosmopolitan]]|last=Venn|first=Lydia|date=15 June 2023|accessdate=16 June 2023}}</ref> The episode was written by series creator [[Charlie Brooker]] and directed by [[David Slade]]. [[Maxine Peake]] stars in the episode as Bella. Joel Collins worked as the production designer.<ref name="indie Collins"/> With Al Green as music editor, the soundtrack features compositions by [[Krzysztof Penderecki]] and includes some pieces which were used in 1980 horror film ''[[The Shining (film)|The Shining]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://salutemag.com/2018/01/03/musical-relevance-black-mirror/|title=The Musical Relevance of Black Mirror|work=Salute|last=Offner|first=Daniel|date=3 January 2018|access-date=7 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180908015838/https://salutemag.com/2018/01/03/musical-relevance-black-mirror/|archive-date=8 September 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="ew interview"/>

===Development===
"Metalhead" was filmed in black and white, a style which had been considered for ''Black Mirror'' before but not previously used.<ref name="variety interview"/> The idea was suggested by the director David Slade to bring to mind old horror films and to match the "oppressive nature" of the episode.<ref name="ew interview"/><ref name="ringer"/> Brooker originally wanted the episode to be entirely free from dialogue,<ref name="ds interview">{{cite web|url=http://www.digitalspy.com/tv/black-mirror/news/a845943/black-mirror-metalhead-season-4-silent-episode/|title=Black Mirror season 4's 'Metalhead' was originally planned as a totally silent episode|work=[[Digital Spy]]|last=Jeffery|first=Morgan|date=29 December 2017|access-date=31 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171231064235/http://www.digitalspy.com/tv/black-mirror/news/a845943/black-mirror-metalhead-season-4-silent-episode/|archive-date=2017-12-31|url-status=live}}</ref> similar to the film ''[[All Is Lost]]''.<ref name="ew interview">{{Cite magazine | url = http://ew.com/tv/2017/12/29/black-mirror-metalhead-interview/ | title = Black Mirror creator explains that 'Metalhead' robot nightmare | first = James | last = Hibbard | date = 29 December 2017 | access-date = 30 December 2017 | magazine = [[Entertainment Weekly]] | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171229164138/http://ew.com/tv/2017/12/29/black-mirror-metalhead-interview/ | archive-date = 2017-12-29 | url-status = live }}</ref> Brooker suggested using the [[Steven Spielberg]] films ''[[Duel (1971 film)|Duel]]'' and ''[[Jaws (film)|Jaws]]'' as inspiration, whilst ''[[The Texas Chain Saw Massacre]]'' was an influence for Slade.<ref name="indie interview"/><ref name="tvguide"/> Executive producer [[Annabel Jones]] felt that the story presented a world devoid of hope, and filming "a world drained of color felt right".<ref name="variety interview">{{Cite web | url = https://variety.com/2017/tv/news/black-mirror-season-4-annabel-jones-interview-1202644294/ | title = 'Black Mirror' Co-Creator Breaks Down Season 4: 'We Want to Be Surprising and Unpredictable' | first = Danielle | last = Turchiano | date = 29 December 2017 | access-date = 1 January 2018 | work = [[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171231233828/http://variety.com/2017/tv/news/black-mirror-season-4-annabel-jones-interview-1202644294/ | archive-date = 2017-12-31 | url-status = live }}</ref> Slade reported that though biological events or apocalypses were considered, the episode does not suggest a backstory for the world in order to focus on the conflict between Bella and the dog.<ref name="tvguide"/>

[[File:David slade eclipse premiere.jpg|thumb|alt=Image of David Slade|"Metalhead" was directed by [[David Slade]].]]

Brooker came up with the episode's central idea while watching videos of [[Boston Dynamics]]' robotics products such as [[BigDog]]. He found that there was something "creepy" in how the products, if knocked over, would look helpless as they worked to regain their stance. Brooker captured this idea in the scene where the dog breaks through the van's back window, but ends up off its legs.<ref name="ibm"/> The dogs have "enough [[artificial intelligence]] to problem solve", according to Slade, and they have no feelings, in contrast to many robots in fiction.<ref name="indie interview"/><ref name="ibm"/> Their design underwent many iterations, the aim being that it should look terrifying, be designed with functionality in mind and kill brutally.<ref name="ibm"/>

Brooker's original script featured a human operating the dog from his home, including a scene where the operator left the "control unit" to give his kids a bath. However, this felt "superfluous", so the intention became for the episode to tell "a very simple story" and hence Brooker pared back the plot.<ref name="ew interview"/> Though viewers may assume the dogs are security for the warehouse, where they are first seen, the intention was for the dogs to have been deployed during a war.<ref name="indie interview"/><ref name="ibm"/> [[Camouflage]] for the dogs was designed but not used.<ref name="indie interview"/> One physical model of a dog was created for the episode, to help give actors and production a concept of their size and shape, but otherwise, all dogs were digitally added in post-production. Visual effects company [[DNEG]] were hired to work on this.<ref name="ibm">{{cite book | title=  Inside Black Mirror | date = November 2018 | first1 = Charlie | last1 = Brooker | first2 = Annabel | last2 = Jones | first3 = Jason | last3 = Arnopp | chapter = Metalhead | isbn = 9781984823489 | publisher =  [[Crown Publishing Group]] | place = New York City }}</ref>

===Filming===
Slade initially received the script in June 2016, while finishing work on the first series of ''[[American Gods (TV series)|American Gods]]''. He was involved in Peake's casting, and had a large amount of autonomy during filming. Extensive location scouting was carried out, with Slade looking for "incredibly soft and overcast" light and "desolation". The 12-day shoot took place in England, largely in [[Devon]] and around [[London]].<ref name="ringer"/><ref name="indie interview"/> With minimal dialogue in the episode, Slade noted that scenes were divided into many brief [[Shot (filmmaking)|shots]], as scenes utilising green screens would be difficult for Peake.<ref name="ringer"/>

Filming took place on two monochrome cameras, not many of which existed at the time. In the scenes with Bella in a car, a remote driver controlled steering from a pod on top of the car. This allowed Peake to act fearfully with more realism. At one point, a dog jumps through a van window and shoots the driver. This sequence was achieved by filming the glass being broken for real, then adding the dog and additional broken glass in post-production.<ref name="ibm"/>

Real [[Lidar]] scans were used to create the scenes shown from the dog's perspective.<ref name="ringer">{{cite web|url=https://www.theringer.com/tv/2017/12/30/16803872/black-mirror-metalhead-david-slade|title='Black Mirror' Watch: Talking to David Slade, the Director of "Metalhead"|last=Herman|first=Alison|work=[[The Ringer (website)|The Ringer]]|date=30 December 2017|access-date=31 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171231212014/https://www.theringer.com/tv/2017/12/30/16803872/black-mirror-metalhead-david-slade|archive-date=2017-12-31|url-status=live}}</ref> Collins came up with the idea that in the scene where the dog escapes the car wreckage, the release of its limb would be similar to the action of a [[drill chuck]]. Collins noted that the dog is "almost humanized" by its movement and damaged arm and compared the dog's multifaceted limbs to [[Pin Art]].<ref name="indie Collins">{{cite web|url=https://www.indiewire.com/2017/12/black-mirror-production-designer-joel-collins-interview-season-4-1201911887/|title='Black Mirror': The Stories Behind Every Season 4 Episode's Most Memorable Pieces of Tech|work=[[IndieWire]]|last=Greene|first=Steve|date=31 December 2017|access-date=7 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180818221221/https://www.indiewire.com/2017/12/black-mirror-production-designer-joel-collins-interview-season-4-1201911887/|archive-date=2018-08-18|url-status=live}}</ref>

The final scene shows a case full of teddy bears, which were yellow in real life but appear white in the episode.<ref name="ew interview"/> Brooker originally considered a gadget such as a [[Game Boy]] instead of a teddy bear, but Slade insisted on "something that you can touch, that you would hold to you, that would give you comfort".<ref name="tvguide">{{cite web|url=https://www.tvguide.com/news/black-mirror-metalhead-ending-david-slade/|title=''Black Mirror''{{'}}s "Metalhead" Almost Had a Different Ending|work=[[TV Guide]]|last=Surette|first=Tim|date=29 December 2017|access-date=7 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180703212259/http://www.tvguide.com/news/black-mirror-metalhead-ending-david-slade/|archive-date=2018-07-03|url-status=live}}</ref> The teddy bears were intended by Slade to be the only "soft and comforting" element of the story.<ref name="ew interview"/>

==Analysis==
"Metalhead" has been described as [[genre fiction]]<ref name="atlantic"/><ref name="vox"/> and [[low concept]].<ref name="digital spy"/> Its tone is one of hopelessness.<ref name="verge">{{cite web|url=https://www.theverge.com/2018/1/5/16853982/black-mirror-metalhead-season-4-maxine-peake-boston-robotics-robot-dog|title=Black Mirror's Metalhead suggests technological disruption is unavoidable (and terminal)|work=[[The Verge]]|last=Bishop|first=Bryan|date=5 January 2018|access-date=5 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180906052446/https://www.theverge.com/2018/1/5/16853982/black-mirror-metalhead-season-4-maxine-peake-boston-robotics-robot-dog|archive-date=2018-09-06|url-status=live}}</ref> The episode is "pared-down and gimmick-free"<ref name="digital spy"/> and has "the most minimal plot in the series".<ref name="telegraph"/> ''[[The Ringer (website)|The Ringer]]''{{'}}s Alison Herman wrote that it is the only episode that cannot be read as an [[allegory]].<ref name="ringer"/> Jacob Stolworthy of ''[[The Independent]]'' suggested that it is the scariest episode of ''Black Mirror'',<ref name="independent"/> while ''[[The Verge]]''{{'}}s Bryan Bishop and his wife were "''literally'' squirming" while watching.<ref name="verge"/> However, ''[[The Atlantic]]'' reviewer David Sims commented that it has little gore when compared with other one-person survival fiction.<ref name="atlantic"/>

===Comparisons===
The episode has widely been described as a simplified version of ''[[The Terminator]]'',<ref name="digital spy"/><ref name="verge"/><ref name="vulture">{{cite web|url=http://www.vulture.com/2017/12/black-mirror-recap-season-4-metalhead.html|title=''Black Mirror'' Recap: Nowhere to Run|work=[[Vulture.com|Vulture]]|last=Bramesco|first=Charles|date=29 December 2017|access-date=5 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180906014118/http://www.vulture.com/2017/12/black-mirror-recap-season-4-metalhead.html|archive-date=2018-09-06|url-status=live}}</ref> a 1984 film which—similar to "Metalhead"—is "about a human run ragged by an android's unceasing pursuit".<ref name="avclub"/> It has also been compared to the "adrenaline highs" of ''[[Mad Max: Fury Road]]'', a 2015 post-apocalyptic film which director [[George Miller (director)|George Miller]] wanted to shoot in black and white.<ref name="vulture"/> Comparisons have also been drawn with the 2016 [[Anohni]] album ''[[Hopelessness (album)|Hopelessness]]'', which "effectively communicates the cold horrors of drone warfare",<ref name="vulture"/> and the [[Philip K. Dick]] short story "[[Second Variety]]".<ref name="avclub"/> Scott Huver of ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' noted that the episode is one of several monochrome works produced around the same time, with others including FX anthology series ''[[Feud (American TV series)|Feud]]'', and "[[Part 8 (Twin Peaks)|Gotta Light?]]" from the 2017 revival of ''Twin Peaks''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://variety.com/2018/tv/features/black-mirror-feud-twin-peaks-crazy-ex-girlfriend-twd-black-and-white-tv-1202689831/|title='Black Mirror,' 'Feud,' 'Twin Peaks' Use Black and White Imagery to Enhance Storytelling|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|last=Huver|first=Scott|date=8 February 2018|access-date=7 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180328072839/http://variety.com/2018/tv/features/black-mirror-feud-twin-peaks-crazy-ex-girlfriend-twd-black-and-white-tv-1202689831/|archive-date=2018-03-28|url-status=live}}</ref> Tim Surette of ''[[TV Guide]]'' compared the episode's horror to past ''Black Mirror'' episodes "[[Playtest (Black Mirror)|Playtest]]" and "[[White Bear (Black Mirror)|White Bear]]".<ref name="tvguide"/>

"Metalhead" contains several [[Easter egg (media)|Easter eggs]]—small details which refer to other ''Black Mirror'' episodes. A postcard and the letters "TCKR" on a truck refer to "[[San Junipero]]", while "Callister" appears on a computer screen in allusion to "[[USS Callister|USS ''Callister'']]".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nme.com/blogs/tv-blogs/black-mirror-season-4-easter-eggs-2204418|title=Did you spot all the Easter Eggs in Black Mirror season 4?|work=[[NME]]|last=Bartleet|first=Larry|date=3 January 2018|access-date=8 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180909000402/https://www.nme.com/blogs/tv-blogs/black-mirror-season-4-easter-eggs-2204418|archive-date=2018-09-09|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.vulture.com/2018/01/black-mirror-season-4-every-easter-egg.html|title=Every Major Easter Egg in ''Black Mirror'' Season Four|work=[[Vulture.com|Vulture]]|last=Tallerico|first=Brian|date=4 January 2018|access-date=8 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180728221541/http://www.vulture.com/2018/01/black-mirror-season-4-every-easter-egg.html|archive-date=2018-07-28|url-status=live}}</ref> When Clarke hijacks a van at the beginning of the episode, text on the car screen refers to previous episodes, as well as containing the message "WHY. did. you. bother. PAUSING. this. you. freak".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mashable.com/2018/01/05/black-mirror-season-4-easter-eggs/|title=13 tiny details in 'Black Mirror' Season 4 you probably missed|work=[[Mashable]]|last=Haysom|first=Sam|date=5 January 2018|access-date=8 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180909000347/https://mashable.com/2018/01/05/black-mirror-season-4-easter-eggs/|archive-date=2018-09-09|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="vice easter">{{cite web|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/every-easter-egg-in-season-four-of-black-mirror/|title=Every Easter Egg Hidden in Season Four of 'Black Mirror'|work=[[Vice (magazine)|Vice]]|last=Mufson|first=Beckett|date=4 January 2018|access-date=8 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180305063007/https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/bjy7j8/every-easter-egg-in-season-four-of-black-mirror|archive-date=2018-03-05|url-status=live}}</ref> The white teddy bears at the end of the episode have been read as a reference to "[[White Bear (Black Mirror)|White Bear]]".<ref name="vice easter"/>

===Themes===
The episode can be seen to explore the [[AI control problem]]: Ed Cumming of ''[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]'' questioned how one could "set limits on [the] ruthlessness" of a robotic guard dog.<ref name="telegraph"/> While watching the episode, Nick Harley of ''Den of Geek'' questioned whether the dogs were self-aware.<ref name="DoG Harley"/> Another ''Den of Geek'' critic, Ryan Lambie, believed the dogs are not [[artificial intelligence]], as their "lack of empathy or emotional nuance" is suggestive of "cold, pre-programmed logic".<ref name="DoG Lambie"/> ''Cultfix''{{'}}s Ryan Monty described the episode as a "pressing statement" on [[autonomous robot|autonomous]] AI and [[drone warfare]].<ref name="cultfix"/> Bishop commented that "Metalhead" may have been conceived with [[Amazon (company)|Amazon]] in mind, particularly its use of drones to carry packages.<ref name="verge"/> Before reaching the final twist, Harley suggested the episode could have been about [[health care]] in a world where medication is government-controlled and guarded by AI.<ref name="DoG Harley"/>

Slade has stated that if there is a theme, it is "how important it is to hold onto our humanity".<ref name="indie interview">{{cite web|url=https://www.indiewire.com/2018/01/black-mirror-metalhead-director-david-slade-robot-dog-interview-1201912565/|title='Black Mirror': 'Metalhead' Director David Slade on the Influences Behind the Season's Most Terrifying Episode|work=[[IndieWire]]|last=Greene|first=Steve|date=2 January 2018|access-date=7 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180728220810/https://www.indiewire.com/2018/01/black-mirror-metalhead-director-david-slade-robot-dog-interview-1201912565/|archive-date=2018-07-28|url-status=live}}</ref> Commenting on the teddy bears, Emily VanDerWerff said in ''[[Vox (website)|Vox]]'' that the message may be that humans are "ruthless in some contexts and quite stupid and soft in others".<ref name="vox"/> According to Scott Beggs of ''[[Nerdist Industries|Nerdist]]'', the episode implies "toys and art are just as vital to survival as the other stuff at the bottom of [[Maslow's hierarchy of needs|Maslow's hierarchy]]".<ref name="nerdist"/> ''[[Digital Spy]]''{{'}}s Steve O'Brien thought the moral is that "there's still room for a tender gesture" in the post-apocalyptic world.<ref name="digital spy">{{cite web|url=http://www.digitalspy.com/tv/black-mirror/review/a845798/black-mirror-metalhead-review-season-4/|title=Black Mirror season 4 'Metalhead' review: This lo-fi thriller is invigoratingly different|work=[[Digital Spy]]|last=O'Brien|first=Steve|date=29 December 2017|access-date=5 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180725214616/http://www.digitalspy.com/tv/black-mirror/review/a845798/black-mirror-metalhead-review-season-4/|archive-date=2018-07-25|url-status=live}}</ref> Bishop believed the story is about the "loss of human innocence" as a sacrifice for progress.<ref name="verge"/> Monty said the episode was about the triumph of "cold, calculated machine effectiveness" over human nature.<ref name="cultfix"/>

Reviewers have commented on early dialogue in the car, when Bella, Anthony and Clarke pass some pigsties. Bishop believed it is a metaphor for [[economic inequality]].<ref name="verge"/> VanDerWerff suggested the scene evokes [[Predation|predator and prey]] imagery, comparing it to [[George Orwell]]'s dystopia ''[[Animal Farm]]''.<ref name="vox"/>

==Reception==
The episode has received mostly positive reviews. On [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the episode has a score of 69% based on 26 reviews. The website's critics consensus reads: "Though 'Metalhead' is the show's shortest installment, the bleakness of its plot and spareness of its thrills can often make it feel longer – though some may appreciate its claustrophobic beauty."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/black_mirror/s04/e05|title=Black Mirror - Season 4, Episode 5 - Rotten Tomatoes|publisher=[[Rotten Tomatoes]]|access-date=20 February 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171204074154/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/black_mirror/s04/e05|archive-date=2017-12-04|url-status=live}}</ref> A ''Cultfix'' review gave the episode a score of eight out of ten.<ref name="cultfix">{{cite web|url=http://cultfix.co.uk/black-mirror-405-review-33049.htm|title=Black Mirror: 405 "Metalhead" Review|work=Cultfix|last=Monty|first=Ryan|date=8 January 2018|access-date=8 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180905024100/http://cultfix.co.uk/black-mirror-405-review-33049.htm|archive-date=2018-09-05|url-status=live}}</ref> The episode received four out of five stars in ''Den of Geek''<ref name="DoG Harley"/> and three out of five stars in ''The Telegraph''.<ref name="telegraph"/> A reviewer for ''[[The A.V. Club]]'' gave the episode a B+ rating.<ref name="avclub"/> Stolworthy believed "Metalhead" is in the "upper echelons" of ''Black Mirror'' episodes,<ref name="independent"/> while Adam Starkey of ''[[Metro (British newspaper)|Metro]]'' summarised it as "an interesting experiment and welcome palette cleanser", though far from the best episode.<ref name="metro">{{cite web|url=https://metro.co.uk/2017/12/31/black-mirror-season-4-metalhead-review-a-hollow-post-apocalyptic-thriller-7193071/|title=Black Mirror season 4 Metalhead review: A hollow post-apocalyptic thriller|work=[[Metro (British newspaper)|Metro]]|last=Starkey|first=Adam|date=31 December 2017|access-date=8 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180506004554/http://metro.co.uk/2017/12/31/black-mirror-season-4-metalhead-review-a-hollow-post-apocalyptic-thriller-7193071/|archive-date=2018-05-06|url-status=live}}</ref> Beggs called the episode "gorgeous but incredibly dull".<ref name="nerdist">{{cite web|url=https://archive.nerdist.com/black-mirrors-metalhead-recap/|title=Black Mirror's "Metalhead" Turns The Apocalypse Upside Down|publisher=[[Nerdist Industries]]|last=Beggs|first=Scott|date=29 December 2017|access-date=8 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180909073552/https://nerdist.com/black-mirrors-metalhead-recap/|archive-date=2018-09-09|url-status=live}}</ref>

Reviewers have widely commented on the episode's 41-minute running time. Sims praised the storyline as "taut", writing that it didn't "waste a moment".<ref name="atlantic"/> Stolworthy said the "relentless" plot makes the episode "feel like the longest" rather than the shortest ''Black Mirror'' episode,<ref name="independent">{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/reviews/black-mirror-season-4-metalhead-review-spoiler-netflix-episode-5-maxine-peake-robot-dog-a8131546.html|title=Black Mirror season 4 episode 5 'Metalhead' spoiler review: Maxine Peake leads scariest episode to date|last=Stolworthy|first=Jacob|work=[[The Independent]]|date=29 December 2017|access-date=5 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180621031935/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/reviews/black-mirror-season-4-metalhead-review-spoiler-netflix-episode-5-maxine-peake-robot-dog-a8131546.html|archive-date=2018-06-21|url-status=live}}</ref> and Monty believed its runtime makes it "one of the most effective and skin-crawling" episodes.<ref name="cultfix"/> Bishop commented that it would have been "untenable" to make the episode longer<ref name="verge"/> and Starkey called the episode's length a "relief" rather than a "detriment".<ref name="metro"/> However, Cumming believed the episode's themes are not enough to sustain it for its running time.<ref name="telegraph"/>

The episode's minimalism was praised by Zack Handlen of ''The A.V. Club'' for its "clear and immediate stakes" and threat which keeps the viewers interested. However, Handlen also claimed that the episode is limited by its simplicity,<ref name="avclub"/> and VanDerWerff criticised it as "exactly the wrong balance between too much information and too little".<ref name="vox"/> ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]''{{'}}s Jacob Oller said that the episode "meanders", and criticised the plot devices as unoriginal.<ref name="paste">{{cite web|url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/articles/2018/01/black-mirror-review-metalhead.html|title=With "Metalhead," ''Black Mirror'' Turns in a Failed Black-and-White Experiment|work=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]|last=Oller|first=Jacob|date=2 January 2018|access-date=8 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180909035556/https://www.pastemagazine.com/articles/2018/01/black-mirror-review-metalhead.html|archive-date=2018-09-09|url-status=live}}</ref>

Stolworthy praised Peake's acting, saying that it "elevates" the episode and increases the viewer's fear of the dog.<ref name="independent"/> Harley praised her performance for allowing the audience to empathise with her character immediately. Harley also complimented the poignancy of Bella's final scene.<ref name="DoG Harley">{{cite web|url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-season-4-episode-5-review-metalhead/|title=Black Mirror Season 4 Episode 5 Review: Metalhead|work=Den of Geek|last=Harley|first=Nick|date=30 December 2017|access-date=5 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180725220635/http://www.denofgeek.com/us/tv/black-mirror/269459/black-mirror-season-4-episode-5-review-metalhead|archive-date=2018-07-25|url-status=live}}</ref> Monty said that "Peake showcases the absolute best of her abilities", playing a character who is "fittingly human and emphatic in her will to survive".<ref name="cultfix"/> Handlen praised her as "easy to root for", saying that Peake "does a good job of finding new ways to be terrified, angry, triumphant, and depressed".<ref name="avclub"/> Cumming wrote that the actor is "never hard to watch" but only has the chance to express degrees of terror.<ref name="telegraph"/>

Bishop commented on the quick pace and wrote that the dog appears "utterly grounded in reality".<ref name="verge"/> Sims praised that "every glimpse of the empty moors in high-contrast black-and-white photography jumps out at the viewer",<ref name="atlantic"/> while Lambie commented positively on the ending's final landscape shots.<ref name="DoG Lambie"/> Harley noted the sparse use of music to create a feeling of dread.<ref name="DoG Harley"/> Monty lauded the lack of exposition in the episode, believing it is the "strongest aspect" as the audience can make individual inferences about the backstory.<ref name="cultfix"/> However, Beggs criticised that the lack of exposition makes it difficult to empathise with Bella.<ref name="nerdist"/>

The ending of "Metalhead" reveals that the warehouse box contained teddy bears. Lambie suggested this is "bleak humour" from Brooker, and another example of the show's exploration of the worst outcomes of new technology.<ref name="DoG Lambie"/> Beggs said the ending was paradoxically both "face-slappingly cheap" and "an outstanding, deeply humane subversion" of apocalypse films.<ref name="nerdist"/> Harley criticised the ending as laughable and not profound.<ref name="DoG Harley"/> Sims criticised it as "perhaps a little too cute"<ref name="atlantic">{{cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2017/12/black-mirrors-metalhead-is-a-short-stylish-survival-thriller/549392/|title=''Black Mirror'': 'Metalhead' Is a Short, Stylish Survival Thriller|work=[[The Atlantic]]|last=Sims|first=David|date=31 December 2017|access-date=5 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180409004520/https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2017/12/black-mirrors-metalhead-is-a-short-stylish-survival-thriller/549392/|archive-date=2018-04-09|url-status=live}}</ref> and VanDerWerff called it "nonsensical", going on to write that it "lands somewhere between affectionate exasperation for humanity's foibles and a sick joke".<ref name="vox">{{cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/culture/2017/12/29/16801992/black-mirror-metalhead-recap-season-4-review|title="Metalhead" is what people who hate Black Mirror hate about Black Mirror|work=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]|last=VanDerWerff|first=Emily|date=29 December 2017|access-date=5 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180906014025/https://www.vox.com/culture/2017/12/29/16801992/black-mirror-metalhead-recap-season-4-review|archive-date=2018-09-06|url-status=live}}</ref> Starkey wrote that the viewer anticipates a revelation about the world or conflict which never comes.<ref name="metro"/>

The dog's design has been praised: Cumming called it "horribly believable".<ref name="telegraph">{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-season-4-metalhead-review-horror-merciless-butthis/|title=Black Mirror, season 4, Metalhead, review: the horror is merciless, the robot dog horribly believable|work=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]|last=Cumming|first=Ed|date=29 December 2017|access-date=5 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180906014246/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-season-4-metalhead-review-horror-merciless-butthis/|archive-date=2018-09-06|url-status=live}}</ref> Lambie called the dog's first appearance in the warehouse  a "superb introduction", and praised the "spiteful and unpredictable" weapons used by the dog.<ref name="DoG Lambie">{{cite web|url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-season-4-metalhead-review/|title=Black Mirror season 4: Metalhead review|work=Den of Geek|last=Lambie|first=Ryan|date=29 December 2017|access-date=5 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180902151811/http://www.denofgeek.com/uk/tv/black-mirror/54117/black-mirror-season-4-metalhead-review|archive-date=2018-09-02|url-status=live}}</ref> Handlen was impressed by the special effects team's dramatisation of "what is essentially a box on legs", commending the "creepily real" design of the dog.<ref name="avclub">{{cite web|url=https://www.avclub.com/the-future-will-not-stop-until-youre-dead-on-a-lean-bla-1821634989|title=The future will not stop until you're dead on a lean ''Black Mirror''|work=[[The A.V. Club]]|last=Handlen|first=Zack|date=29 December 2017|access-date=5 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180906014207/https://www.avclub.com/the-future-will-not-stop-until-youre-dead-on-a-lean-bla-1821634989|archive-date=2018-09-06|url-status=live}}</ref> Contrastingly, Oller found the dog's design and animation simplistic, commenting that it is "not the imposing, minimalist murder machine it needs to be". Oller found that the monochrome gave the scenery an "especially unreal sheen".<ref name="paste"/>

===Awards===
